currentContext.business: BPCL refines crude oil at three refineries (Mumbai, Kochi and Bina) with a stated refining capacity of 35.3 MMTPA and markets an integrated portfolio of Fuels, Lubricants, LPG, Natural Gas, Convenience Retail and Digital Services through a nationwide network of over 25,000 fuel stations and more than 6,200 LPG distributors. It serves both retail customers and bulk consumers including the Defence Forces, Indian Railways, state government bodies, state transport undertakings, airlines and power producers, and pursues upstream oil and gas through its wholly owned subsidiary Bharat PetroResources Limited. The Company describes itself as expanding across biofuels, renewable energy, electric mobility and green hydrogen alongside the conventional core. currentContext.mdna: India's petroleum product consumption reached 243.2 MMT in FY 2025-26, up 1.7%, driven by transportation fuels and LPG: motor spirit +6.5%, LPG +6.0%, high-speed diesel +3.6%, ATF +2.0%; petcoke, naphtha and other products declined.|Structural mix shift toward petrol: over FY 2015-16 to FY 2025-26 MS grew at a 6.9% CAGR, LPG 5.4%, ATF 3.9% and HSD 2.4%, taking the HSD-to-MS consumption ratio down to 2.2 from 3.6 a decade ago - management attributes this to rising private vehicle ownership and passenger mobility.|Import dependence rose: crude oil import dependence increased to 88.7% from 88.2% and LPG import dependence to 61% from 59%, while natural gas import dependence fell to 49.2% from 50.1%.|Crude cost tailwind for most of the year: Brent averaged $70.5/bbl in FY 2025-26 versus $78.9/bbl (down 10.6%) and the Indian Basket averaged $71.0/bbl versus $78.58/bbl (down 9.6%).|A late-year supply shock reversed that: closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a corridor handling around 20% of global oil and LNG trade - drove Brent from around $71/bbl at end-February 2026 to over $127/bbl by end-March, peaking above $144/bbl in early April, with refining margins and product prices surging particularly for middle distillates; the IEA coordinated an emergency release of approximately four hundred million barrels from strategic petroleum reserves.|LNG market re-tightening: damage to Qatar's liquefaction infrastructure disrupted approximately 17% of that country's export capacity with repairs expected to take three to five years and could reduce cumulative global LNG supply by around 120 bcm during 2026-2030; WIM rose ~143% and JKM ~138% from end-February to early March 2026 and both remained roughly 65-70% above pre-crisis levels in May 2026, with LNG freight rates up more than 40%.|Global oil demand growth is slowing structurally - up 0.65 mb/d (0.7%) in 2025 versus 0.75 mb/d in CY 2024 and well below the 2010-2019 average of 1.4 mb/d - on weaker petrochemical feedstock demand in China, EV adoption and efficiency gains.|EVs are the primary source of structural oil demand displacement: global EV sales exceeded 20 million units in 2025 (around 25% of new vehicle sales), are projected at 23 million in 2026 (approaching 30%), with penetration expected to exceed 40% by 2030 and the IEA estimating displacement of approximately 5 mb/d of oil demand by 2030, primarily gasoline.|Petrochemicals is expected to be the single largest contributor to global oil demand growth through 2030, and integrated refining-petrochemical complexes are expected to be critical to long-term competitiveness and margin stability - the explicit rationale for BPCL's petrochemical pivot.|Capital is rotating away from upstream oil: global upstream oil investment is projected to decline for a third consecutive year in 2026 to below $500 billion, while natural gas investment rises to approximately $330 billion, the highest in a decade; total global energy investment is projected up 5% to $3.4 trillion in 2026 ($2.2 trillion clean energy, $1.2 trillion oil/gas/coal).|India's refining sector: nameplate capacity of 258.1 MMTPA across 22 refineries (private sector ~34.3%), crude throughput of 272.1 MMT and average utilisation of 105% in FY 2025-26; the government targets 309.5 MMTPA by FY 2029-30.|Domestic supply is shrinking: domestic crude oil and condensate production fell 3.2% to 27.9 MMT and domestic natural gas production fell 3.7% to 34.8 BCM, with indigenous crude processed meeting only around 11.3% of total petroleum product consumption.|Upstream policy opening: OALP Rounds X and XI offer approximately 262,817 sq km of acreage supporting a government objective of attracting around $100 billion of upstream investment, with India aiming to expand exploration acreage to 1 million sq km by FY 2029-30.|Gas demand mix: natural gas consumption declined 3.0% to 69.0 BCM on lower industrial demand, but City Gas Distribution consumption grew 9.7% and is the stated key growth driver; the product pipeline network spans 24,861 km with 155.8 MMTPA capacity operating at 68.4% utilisation.|Macro backdrop for FY 2026-27: IMF and RBI project India GDP growth of 6.5% and 6.4% respectively with inflation rising to 5.1% from 2.1%, amid persistent geopolitical uncertainty and elevated energy prices; risks.risk: Crude price and energy supply-route shock from geopolitical conflict
risks.note: The single dominant risk in this report. The escalation of the West Asia conflict and, for the first time in history, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz - a corridor handling around 20% of global oil and LNG trade - drove Brent from around $71/bbl at end-February 2026 to over $127/bbl by end-March and a peak above $144/bbl in early April, alongside sharply higher tanker freight rates, marine insurance costs and shipping expenses. The Directors' Report records that after March 31, 2026 these developments continued to cause volatility in crude prices, freight, insurance and foreign exchange (the sentence is cut off mid-clause in the routed text). BPCL buys crude into a market where India's crude oil import dependence rose to 88.7% and LPG import dependence to 61%, so the exposure is structural rather than episodic.

risks.risk: Climate change - both physical damage and transition risk (BRSR material issue #1, classified a Risk)
risks.note: BPCL states that floods and extreme weather pose direct risks to its refining and marketing operations, logistics and supporting infrastructure, while transition risks arise as it advances decarbonisation - changes in regulation, market conditions and technology 'may affect the value of current assets and require faster investment in alternative energy solutions'. The Company itself describes negative financial implications: asset damage, higher maintenance costs and unexpected downtime; regulatory restrictions on products such as Light Diesel Oil and Furnace Oil reducing petroleum product sales; underuse of existing refining and distribution assets; lower returns on conventional energy infrastructure; and the need to allocate additional capital to green hydrogen, renewable procurement and decarbonisation technologies. The stated mitigation is a decarbonisation pathway targeting Net-Zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2040.

risks.risk: Structural demand displacement from electrification and the energy transition
risks.note: Management's own MD&A quantifies the erosion of its core product demand: global oil demand growth slowed to 0.65 mb/d (0.7%) in 2025 against a 2010-2019 average of 1.4 mb/d; global EV sales exceeded 20 million units in 2025 (around 25% of new vehicle sales), are projected at 23 million in 2026 (approaching 30%) and penetration is expected to exceed 40% by 2030; the IEA estimates EV adoption could displace approximately 5 mb/d of oil demand by 2030, primarily gasoline. The BRSR separately records 'Energy use and transition' as a material issue, acknowledging that delays in adapting 'could lead to higher costs, regulatory exposure, and the risk of stranded assets'. Motor spirit is BPCL's second-largest product by turnover, so gasoline displacement bears directly on the mix.

risks.risk: Extreme product and activity concentration in refined petroleum
risks.note: A structural concentration the BRSR discloses without labelling it a risk: 100% of turnover comes from a single main activity, 'Manufacture of coke and refined petroleum products'. Within that, High Speed Diesel contributes 46.72% and Motor Spirit 27.46% of total turnover - roughly three-quarters of revenue in two fuels - with LPG at 11.76%, ATF at 3.20% and CNG at 1.84%. Exports are only 1.39% of turnover and international operations number zero plants and zero offices, so there is essentially no geographic diversification to offset an Indian regulatory, demand or pricing shock. (Product-mix percentages back-filled from BRSR Section A routed to the registry and governance_entities bundles.)

risks.risk: Rupee depreciation against a dollar-denominated import bill
risks.note: The Rupee closed FY 2025-26 at Rs 94.65 to the US dollar, down 10.6% from the previous year-end and among the weaker Asian currencies, with the annual average at Rs 88.31 (a 4.4% year-on-year depreciation). Because roughly 88.7% of India's crude is imported and priced in dollars, currency weakness raises landed input cost independently of the crude price itself; the report also records FPI outflows of around Rs 1.5 lakh crore and a fall in reserves from a peak of $728.5 billion to around $688 billion. The Directors' Report explicitly lists foreign exchange movements among the post-year-end volatility factors.

risks.risk: Occupational health and safety across refining, pipeline and retail operations (BRSR material issue #12, classified a Risk)
risks.note: BPCL identifies workplace accidents, injuries and non-compliance with regulatory requirements as risks that may affect employee well-being and result in financial loss, reputational impact and reduced employee engagement, with failure to maintain a safe working environment potentially leading to legal liabilities and regulatory penalties. Mitigation is framed around the 'Safety First, Safety Must' principle and structured hazard identification, extended to customers through product and service safety standards. Scale amplifies exposure: alongside 6,734 employees the Company engages an average contract labour strength of 32,567, and it operates 281 plants.

risks.risk: Environmental compliance exposure across water, waste and biodiversity (BRSR material issues #4, #5 and #8, all classified Risks)
risks.note: Water: a key input for refining and cooling, with stated risks of shortages, pollution incidents and regulatory non-compliance affecting operational continuity; BPCL reduced total water withdrawal from 56,366.30 TKL in FY 2024-25 to 50,909.25 TKL in FY 2025-26, operates Bina Refinery as a Zero Liquid Discharge facility which recycled and reused 11,544.83 TKL, and used 473.66 TKL of harvested rainwater. Waste: oily sludge, spent catalysts, spent clay, e-waste and solid waste, where improper management can bring legal liability and suspension or cancellation of authorisations by State and Central Pollution Control Boards. Biodiversity: refining, pipeline and land-based operations across varied ecosystems, where inadequate safeguards can cause habitat degradation, regulatory challenge, community resistance and reputational impact.

risks.risk: Board composition non-compliance - no Independent Directors from end-March 2026
risks.note: Back-filled from the Corporate Governance report routed to the profile and governance_entities bundles: the tenure of all four Independent Directors, including the sole woman Independent Director, ceased during March 2026, leaving a six-member Board of four Whole-time Directors and two Government Nominee Directors with zero women (0.00% of the Board). BPCL states it has taken up the matter with the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas for nomination of the requisite number of Independent Directors to fulfil Regulation 17(1) of the Listing Regulations and Section 149 of the Companies Act, 2013 - meaning the composition of the Audit Committee and other statutory committees depends on a government nomination outside the Company's control. The Directors' Report also records that Independent Director performance evaluation is done by the Administrative Ministry, not the Board.

themes.title: Oil & Gas - gas economy (CGD/LNG) + refining/upstream
themes.need: India's gas-economy push now collides with an outright policy reversal. ATGL grew volume 13% to 303 MMSCM and revenue 27% to INR 1,908cr, yet EBITDA FELL sequentially to INR 281cr (~14.7% margin, from INR 310cr) because the government withdrew the pooled-gas mechanism after the West Asia 'peace deal', pushing ATGL to ~15% spot volumes with Brent above $107/bbl; management also noted NWG price is 12% of the Indian crude basket, so a 62% domestic mix protects far less than it looks, and CNG station adds slowed to +5 from +25 in Q4 even as CNG demand grows ~30%. The same shock ran the other way for integrated refining: RELIANCE delivered O2C EBITDA of INR 17,000cr (+17%) THROUGH the Strait-of-Hormuz closure at 96-97% throughput while Asian peers ran 15-20% below capacity, with ethane+ROGC at ~70% of ethylene feed as distillate cracks blew out (gas oil $16 to $63, ATF $14 to $62). MGL/GUJGASLTD/IGL/IRMENERGY carry the same CGD margin squeeze; PETRONET/OIL/ONGC/IOC ride LNG-infra + domestic-gas; CHENNPETRO/MRPL ride GRM cracks; DEEPINDS/JINDRILL/SEAMECLTD on ONGC E&P capex; AEGISLOG/AEGISVOPAK add LPG/gas terminalling.
themes.driver: Whether the pooled/APM gas-allocation mechanism is restored (the single biggest CGD earnings variable); LNG spot price and Brent; GRM/distillate cracks; ONGC rig tenders & day-rates.
